appraisal_events.evidence: On his mistress's word he drops devoted relatives "qui la méritaient le moins"; he spends most of his time on letters and telegrams, and when she picks a quarrel from a distance the narrator reads it "de sa figure décomposée"; he writes "Dis-moi ce que j'ai fait de mal. Je suis prêt à reconnaître mes torts", grief persuading him he was at fault, while she keeps him waiting for answers "dénuées de sens" and he comes back from the post office "le front soucieux et bien souvent les mains vides".
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage shows him wholly at the disposal of a woman who withholds explanation and even affection, to the point of manufacturing his own guilt; the leverage in the relation is entirely hers.

appraisal_events.evidence: Seeing her joyful about Saint-Loup's offer to photograph her, in "sa plus belle toilette" and hesitating among coiffures, he is "un peu irrité de cet enfantillage" and wonders "si je ne m'étais pas trompé sur ma grand'mère, si je ne la plaçais pas trop haut", whether she had "de la coquetterie".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator locally revises her downward from detachment to vanity, but the passage frames the suspicion as an astonished young man's revision of a lifetime's evidence, tilting the doubt back onto the one who doubts.

status_effects.explanation: He needs, begs, waits and confesses faults he has not committed, while the other party withholds everything; his dependence is the passage's dominant movement.
In the narrator's private estimate she drops from disinterested elevation to suspected coquetry — an unshared judgment, and one the narration itself holds at arm's length.

ambiguities: The grandmother's own motive for the photograph is never given here, and the doubt about her is voiced as a question the narrator came to ask ('si je ne m'étais pas trompé'), so the diminishment may belong to the observer rather than to her.
